body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The New Comedy of Sons of Erin, or Modern Sentiment. This little theatre continues to rise in superiority over its huge rival, with respect to the production of new pieces. Yesterday week it presented us with one of the best comedies that has appeared for some time. It is called the Sons of Erin, or Modern Sentiment, and is said to be from the pen of Mrs. Lefanu, sister of Mr. Sheridan, a lady who might reasonably be expected to have a portion of genius about her, being literary on every side of relationship—ship, brother’s, father’s, mother’s, grandfather’s, and great-grandfather’s. The story is simple and pleasing. Fitz-Edward (De Camp), a young Irish gentleman, clandestinely marries into a family who have an antipathy to his countrymen, and having soon reduced his fortune to nothing by his inexperience and reckless generosity, is reduced to the necessity of looking about him for a subsistence. Coming to England for this purpose, and meeting accidentally with a young lady of quality, his cousin (Miss Duncan), she recommends him, under a concealed name, as an amanuensis to Miss Ruth Rivers, an elderly and learned maiden, who is his father-in-law's sister, and resides with the very family from which his wife’s marriage had alienated her. They are, of course, unacquainted with the person of their new inmate, who is represented as an amiable as well as an honourable man; and the consequence is, that after a short time, he not only becomes the confident of Mr. Rivers (Powell), and succeeds in extricating Mrs. Rivers, his young second wife (Mrs. Edwin), from a dangerous sentimental intimacy with a libertine of fashion, but engages the tender affections of Miss Ruth herself, and so recommends himself in every way to every member of the family, that they are all agreed in wishing he was one of the family, and exclaim, what a different thing it would have been, if their daughter had married such a man as this! At this fortunate juncture, Mrs. Fitz-Edward (Miss Boyce), comes over to join her husband in England, and after meeting with some little jealous vexations, owing to the blunders of an Irish servant (Johnstone), who had wondered at the intimacy between his master and his fair cousin, and to the partial perusal of a letter which falls into her hands, is enabled to make her peace with the family in consequence of the good offices of a generous old uncle (Dowton). It is however not a very cordial one, for they are all under a delusion with regard to the character of her husband, who is supposed to have added to his national offences by deserting her. Miss Ruth, in the mean time, has made actual proposals of marriage to her amanuensis, who in receiving them equivocally contrives to procure from her a written testimonial of her good opinion; and thus secured against all objection, he makes his appearance in the final scene. The sight of his wife rouses all the tenderness and enthusiasm of his heart, and raising his head and opening his arms with an effusion of conjugal love, the enraptured antique takes the address to herself and opens her arms likewise, when to her utter dismay as well as to the delighted surprise of all present, he rushes by her into the embrace of her niece. Miss Ruth, upon her recovery, starts some little difficulty at first upon receiving the sad fellow directly into her confidence, but a little side explanation between her and the gentleman, who with a graceful spirit returns the written character she gave him, converts her angry tones into a faltering though complete testimony to his merits, and the all-conquering Hibernian is left, unobstructed and acknowledged, to the enjoyment of his well-earned remunerations. There are no very striking or bold marks of dramatic genius about these incidents, nor indeed about the characters or language of the piece; but it has a very decided superiority over the general run of modern comedies in a certain air of good-breeding which is diffused over it; there is also a great deal of sound sense exhibited in the formation of the characters; the language, though not to be compared with that of Mr. Sheridan's comedies in terseness and pregnancy, is polite and appropriate; and the main feature of the story is, to me at least, an original one. The sound sense, to which I allude as exhibited in the characters, regards not only their general management, which bears evident proof of a right attention to nature, but such parts in particular as give the piece its second title of Modern Sentiment,—to wit, a libertine full of a selfish non-chalance, who inveigles a married woman into an imaginary platonism,—the lady who is thus inveigled by means of her vanity, enlivened perhaps with a little consciousness of her comparative youthfulness as a wife,—and a plain spoken, warm-hearted old gentleman, the uncle above-mentioned, who is evidently brought forward by way of contrast to the usual ridiculous idea of generosity on the stage, and neither gives away hundreds to every beggar he meets, nor chuses to have what he does give considered as any thing extraordinary. The exercise of a well-directed and rational charity he justly considers as a duty, the omission of which is very wicked, while the performance of it is nothing very virtuous; and accordingly, while he acts up heartily to his benevolence, he is rather pained and humiliated than otherwise to hear himself applauded for so doing. There is something extremely solid, as well as attractive, in the idea of this character, and highly calculated to raise one’s respect for the mind that formed it. The other and principal title, The Sons of Erin, points out the laudable and seasonable intention of the fair writer to do away the lingering prejudices with regard to the character of her countrymen. It is well imagined and pursued; and though nothing is really proved in favour of a country or a set of opinions by setting them off to advantage in the person of an accomplished hero, since any country or set of opinions may be well or ill painted on this principle, yet it is quite justifiable and proper to overturn gross and unmixed prejudices by favourable specimens of what they condemn; and while the frank and cordial features of Irish character will never want a proper appreciation from sensible people, those who condemn without having studied them, will find sufficient answer and refutation in the national portraits of Mrs. Lefanu.

With the exception of De Camp, who with his feeble thick voice and insignificant manner always makes a sorry figure in upper parts, the principal characters are justly performed. Dowton throws his usual fine breadth of feeling into the sound-hearted uncle, who disdains affectation and flattery. Miss Duncan has a good opportunity, as a lively and elegant young widow, of shewing her skill in distinguishing high spirits from a noisy vulgarity. Johnstone, with his air of sturdy simplicity and trusting good humour, is all his old whim and quaintness in the Irish servant. Wrench is good in the indifferent man of fashion, which just suits his careless outline of style. Even Miss Boyce, in her Irish husband, has found a Pygmalion at last to warm her into life, and is really something more than a pretty statue in the scene where she reads the letter. It is a pity she cannot get rid of her trick of frowning, which spoils a nice set of features, and a turn of head and countenance that might be made very winning and picturesque. But as to Mrs. Edwin, who has talents enough to excite one’s best wishes for her success, she has indulged herself to such an excess in a certain deep and pithy tone of importance, with which she delivers out her words like a lecture, that she has quite lost sight of that natural mode of speaking and various familiarity, which at former times she has appeared so well to understand. Whenever she looks gravely, and is going to speak, with her head on one side and her finger raised up, she seems about to utter the same sort of words, and to deal forth such phrases as, "Let me tell you, Mr. Jenkins," or, "Really, it is incumbent on me to assure you, Mr. Blenkinsop."—Let her think of this fault, with the good sense she appears to possess, and learn how to obtain more effect by toiling after less.

The piece, thus written and thus performed, goes off with the success it deserves. Some political allusions are eagerly caught up by the audience; and the following in particular has obtained three distinct rounds of applause:—“In families, as in governments, make sure of the women, and your business is done.”
